hook: Trying harder to start a task makes it harder to start. This is not intuitive, but it's accurate.
topic: The threat response — how forcing effort increases resistance
body:
**Trying harder to start a task makes it harder to start. I know that's not intuitive. But it's accurate.**

When you grit your teeth, focus your will, and attempt to force yourself into a task, your brain registers that internal pressure as threat signalling. The part of your brain responsible for threat detection doesn't know the difference between external danger and the self-generated pressure of trying to override avoidance. It responds the same way — by increasing resistance.

This is why the harder you try to make yourself do the thing, the more exhausted you feel before you've even started. The effort is real. It's just directed at the wrong target.

You're not building momentum. You're triggering a defensive response that makes the task feel more aversive than it did before you tried to force it.

The reframe: the goal is not to force a start — it is to reduce the perceived cost of starting until the action becomes easier than the resistance.

One action: the next time you notice you're forcing, stop. Take 90 seconds, stand up, move — then return to the task with zero expectation of quality. You're not starting the real work. You're just opening the file.
